newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts lapped up at first auction of the year.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts lapped up at first auction of the year.

text.p: Investors queued up to buy at the first Bank of England gilt auction of 1997 on Tuesday and demand for the 10-year bonds was more than double the 2.5 billion pounds on offer.
The Bank of England said its auction of 2.5 bln pounds of 7.25 percent gilts due 2007 was covered 2.17 times.
"That represents good depth of cover," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson. "The market dipped initially because there was a bit of a tail but it should recover from here."
The auction had a yield tail of just one basis point -- the distance between the average yield and highest yield accepted at auction. The price tail was 4/32.
A longer tail would have suggested that the Bank was forced to accept lower offers to sell the bonds.
The March gilt future was trading 10/32 lower on the day at 110-00 straight after the auction and had crept up to 110-02 by 1130 GMT.

Traders breathed a sigh of relief and said the auction may have finally laid to rest the spectre of the 10-year gilt tender back in September 1995 which failed to attract full cover -- the first time ever that a British government bond auction had failed to generate sufficient demand.
"There have always been jitters about 10-year auctions since then," Scott said.
Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW, said a number of factors had favoured Tuesday's sale.

"The market benefited from having cheapened up in spread terms against the other European markets over the past week and of course the currency dropped as well. That probably attracted a little bit of buying," he told Reuters Financial Television.

The pound has backed off its heady heights in recent days, dropping about eight pfennigs against the mark from last week's high to a low of 2.6415 on Monday, after a run of UK economic data took pressure off Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates immediately.

The gilt/Bund spread -- the premium which international investors demand for buying British bonds rather than German government bonds -- has also widened, from well below 180 basis points at the start of last week, to 185 on Tuesday.
The good showing at Tuesday's auction augurs well for Thursday's sale of 1.5 billion pounds of 7.0 percent gilts due 2002.
"The five year on Thursday should go quite well. that's an area that appeals to foreign investors," said Peter Osler, economist at GNI.
Scott agreed, noting the relatively small amount of bonds on offer. "Ten-years never go as well as five-years, so today's result is really pretty good."
The other side of the gilt supply equation -- namely the state of Britain's public sector finances -- also appears to be going the market's way.

"The last three or four figures have been quite encouraging for the PSBR (budget deficit) outlook and I think there is a very good chance that we'll get a better result for the fiscal year than the Chancellor is going for," Osler said.
"In that respect, the outlook for gilts and for supply is quite positive."
In his November budget, Clarke forecast a total public sector borrowing requirement of 26.4 billion pounds for the current financial year.
But the lower that figure proves to be, the fewer gilts the Bank of England will have to sell to a saturated bond market.
